runs.text: Huns pilouros que fazem de pò de cer-

lines.note: Tandon names small pellets made from the powder of a particular charcoal. The printed cer- continues as to on the following physical line; the headword remains roman.

runs.text: to caruão que poem nos perfumadores os quaes

lines.note: The charcoal pellets are placed in perfume burners. This line completes certo from the preceding line and introduces the relative clause describing how long the pellets burn.
The pellets remain alight for a long time, completing the Tandon definition. The vowel read as u in durão is abraded; that incorporated reading fits both its visible remnant and the sense.
Tane means seed. The pilcrow introduces Tanega cauaru, whose explanation concerns children of differing paternity; Se- continues as rem on the next line.

runs.text: rem dous, ou mais filhos da meſma mãy, &

lines.note: The example describes two or more children of the same mother. The final conjunction links this line to the different-father qualification below; mãy retains its printed nasal mark.
The parentage example ends with different fathers. A new pilcrow introduces Taneuo tatçu, destroying the seed; the Portuguese Dei- continues as tar on the next line.

runs.text: tar a perder a ſemẽte. Itẽ, permet deſtruir de

lines.note: Deitar a perder means to ruin the seed; the entry also extends this metaphorically to complete destruction. The printed abbreviation and nasal marks are retained without expanding the canonical text.
The first word completes the preceding total-destruction sense. Taneuo maqu begins a separate example of sowing by scattering, with espa- continuing on the following line.
The scattering example ends here. Taneuo voroſu introduces giving seed to cultivators; the explanation continues with the landowner as the giver.

runs.text: o ſenhor, ou dono das terras ſemẽte empreſtada

lines.note: The landowner supplies seed as a loan. This continues the example introduced above, rather than defining a new Japanese item; the nasal abbreviation in ſemẽte is retained.

runs.text: aos lauradores pera ſemear, ou repartila o q̃

lines.note: The borrowed seed is for farmers to sow, or is distributed by their headman. The printed q̃ abbreviates que and is retained rather than silently expanded.

runs.text: he cabeça dos lauradores pellos que a não tem.

lines.note: This completes the alternative distribution arrangement: the head of the cultivators shares seed among those who lack it. Cabeça is figurative leadership, not an anatomical reference.
Taneuo caſu introduces soaking seed in water. The medial letter is long s, not f; nagoa remains joined as printed, and pe- continues below.

runs.text: ra amolecer, & ficar deſposta pera ſemear

lines.note: The soaking softens the seed and prepares it for sowing. This is uninterrupted Portuguese explanatory text, with the historical spelling deſposta retained.
The final phrase specifies sowing in the ground and closes the long Tane entry. It remains an indented continuation, not a separate entry.
This Tanen means many years, also expressed by the roman Japanese gloss Vouoi toxi. It is a separate homograph from the following entry about other thoughts.
The second Tanen denotes other thoughts or thinking about other matters. The Portuguese sentence continues on the next physical line; its headword is not merged with the preceding homograph.
The visible spacing in co iſas is retained. The Japanese example means to say one's prayer without distracting thoughts; Oraciouo is wholly roman, and mǒ- continues below.

runs.text: Orai ſem cuidar outras couſas, ou ſem

lines.note: The fragment xe completes mǒxe. The Portuguese imperative asks the reader to pray without thinking about other things, with an alternative phrasing continuing below.
The closing phrase restates the instruction not to be distracted in thought. It completes the prayer example and the second Tanen entry.
Tango is explained by the Japanese expression Goguat itçuca. The Portuguese dates it to the fifth day, with the relevant lunar month specified on the following line.
The date is the fifth day of the fifth lunar month. The source's lua, ou mes wording is preserved rather than converted into a Gregorian date.
Tangua, alternatively Tanguaya, denotes a lodging establishment compared to a hospital. The following line specifies its guests; the historical comparison need not imply a modern medical institution.
The lodging receives travelling Buddhist monks. A pilcrow then introduces a Japanese example beginning Tan-, whose continuation belongs to the same word on the following line.
The initial fragment completes Tanguayano. The example compares a house or place to such a lodging; the Portuguese co- continues as mo below.

runs.text: mo hoſpital onde concorre muita gente de vari-

lines.note: The comparison is to a lodging where many people gather from various places. The source's vari- continues on the next line, without creating a separate lexical unit.
This completes varias partes, referring to the different places from which visitors come. It closes the extended example under Tangua.
Tanguaya is a cross-reference to Tangua immediately above. Vide is italic Portuguese editorial text, while both Japanese headword forms remain roman.
This Tani means valley. It is a complete short entry and must remain separate from the identically written headword for a tick on the next line.
This homograph is defined as a tick. The source writes Tani; it is not silently modernized to a different contemporary romanization.

runs.text: Ribeiro, ou ribeira dagoa, que vai

lines.note: Tanigaua denotes a stream running between valleys. The printed dagoa remains joined, and the relative clause continues on the next physical line.
This continuation specifies that the stream runs among valleys. It closes Tanigaua before the separate, previously omitted Taniguchi entry.
The scan contains a complete omitted entry here: Taniguchi, the mouth or entrance of a valley. A new stable suffix ID restores this physical row without renumbering later lines.
Tanin is glossed by Betno fito and described as another person who is not a relative. The final qualification continues below; the Japanese gloss stays roman.
Parente completes the definition of Tanin as someone outside one's kin. This single-word physical line is an indented continuation, not an independent entry.
Tan-in is a distinct hyphenated headword for an illness associated with phlegm. The historical medical wording is transcribed, not offered as a modern diagnosis.
Taninju means many people or a large number of people. The scan presents a self-contained headword and short Portuguese definition on this line.
Taninoto is equated with Tani, valley. The terminal roman P. is the source's poetic-use label; it does not belong to the Portuguese definition or the Japanese headword.
Tanixi denotes snails associated with flooded fields. The historical spelling varzeas is preserved, without adding a species identification absent from the source.
Tanja, also Tanxa, names a red powdered substance. Its uses as colouring or medicine continue on the following line; both Japanese variants remain roman.

runs.text: ſeruẽ de tinta vermelha clara, ou de mezinha.

lines.note: The red powder serves as a light red pigment or a medicinal preparation. The source's historical use is reported without endorsing the substance as a present-day treatment.

runs.text: Verſos eſcritos em tira de papel.

lines.note: Tanjacu denotes verses written on a strip of paper. The entire Portuguese definition fits on this physical line and closes the entry.
Tanjei, alternatively qixei, means supplications. Vt introduces an example whose headword is divided Tan- / jeiuo across the line boundary.
The fragment jeiuo completes Tanjeiuo in an expression for earnest supplication. The Portuguese depreca- continues as ções on the next line.
The final words describe making supplications intensely or earnestly. They complete both the divided Portuguese word and the example under Tanjei.
Tanji gives verbal forms for playing a stringed instrument. The example Biuauo tan- continues across the column boundary as zuru; the printed division is preserved.
Zuru completes the example begun at the bottom of the left column. The Portuguese compares playing the biwa to playing a viola; this is not a new headword.
Tanjit, glossed by Mijicai fi, refers to short days. Both Japanese expressions are roman, followed by the italic Portuguese definition.
This Tanjǒ is defined as something beautiful. The example Xenqen tan- continues below and is distinct from the birth-related homograph that follows.
The fragment jǒna completes the example Xenqen tanjǒna. Idem repeats the preceding beautiful-thing sense and closes this first Tanjǒ entry.
The second Tanjǒ concerns birth, with Vmare, uru as a Japanese verbal gloss. The expression Tanjǒ ſu- continues on the next line.
Ru completes ſuru, to be born or give birth. The example mentions Saint Mary; the heavily printed mark in võcouo is incorporated as a nasal tilde, though its damaged shape is nonblocking uncertainty.
This completes the Japanese example and its Portuguese translation, Saint Mary gave birth to a son. The abbreviated nasal spellings are retained instead of modernized.

runs.text: Lugar do nacimento, ou caſa onde

lines.note: Tanjóya denotes a birthplace or the house where someone gave birth. The visible accent looks like a single acute stroke; ó records that appearance rather than normalizing it to adjacent ǒ forms.
The closing words identify the house where someone gave birth. This is an indented continuation of Tanjóya and completes its Portuguese explanation.
Tanmat means beginning and end, with Fajimeto, ſuye as the Japanese gloss. The source punctuation and conjunction are retained.
Tanmei denotes a short life, also expressed as Mijicai inochi. This compact entry is complete on one physical line.
Tanna is referred to the preferred form Tazzuna for reins. The editorial l, potiùs is italic as printed, and the Portuguese definition continues below.
Caualo specifies that the reins are for a horse. This single-word continuation closes the Tanna entry and its reference to Tazzuna.
Tanne is referred to the preferred verbal form Tazzune, to ask or seek. The nasal abbreviation and the printed division Pergũ- are retained.
This completes the Portuguese definition as asking or searching. It belongs to Tanne and does not introduce a separate Japanese form.
Tanô denotes many skills or good qualities. The example is divided Ta- / nôna across physical lines; the circumflex is retained.
The fragment completes Tanôna fito, a person with many abilities. The Portuguese enumeration continues on the next line and remains part of this example.
The closing phrase adds good arts or accomplishments to the person's abilities. It completes the example and the Tanô entry.
Tanome refers to another man's wife. Vt introduces an example beginning Tanomeuo; its verb and Portuguese explanation continue on the next line.
Vocaſu completes the Japanese example, translated as committing adultery with a married woman. The long s is retained in the canonical verb.
This noun Tanomi means a request or trust. The first example begins Tano- and continues below; it is separate from the later verbal entry.
The divided phrase completes Tanomiuo caquru, placing trust and hope in someone. The Portuguese eſperã- continues on the following line.

runs.text: ça em alguem. ¶ Item, Preſente que ſe

lines.note: The trust example ends with someone as its object. Item introduces a further sense, a present given in connection with a marriage arrangement.

runs.text: manda como arras em ſinal dos deſpoſorios.

lines.note: The present is sent as a betrothal pledge. This continues the additional noun sense under Tanomi rather than beginning a new headword.
The expressions Tanomiuo yaru and vocuru introduce sending the betrothal gifts. The closely set l,vocuru and nasal abbreviation in Mãdar are preserved.

runs.text: arras, ou dar ſinal como penhor pera comprar,

lines.note: The explanation extends from betrothal gifts to giving a deposit or pledge in a transaction. Its buying-or-selling construction continues onto the next line.
This completes the reference to a pledge for buying or selling something. It closes the extended noun entry Tanomi before the separate verb.
The verbal Tanomi gives its inflected forms and means to request help or entrust oneself. The object of the Portuguese phrase follows below.
The verb involves appealing to someone. Sonatauo tanomu introduces a direct request; its Portuguese translation is divided Ro- / go across the line boundary.

runs.text: go vos, que me concedais tal couſa, ou me fa-

lines.note: The speaker asks the addressee to grant something or provide help. The final fa- continues as uoreçais on the following physical line.
The request example closes with asking for favour. A further sense, trusting, begins an example divided To- / xino across lines.
The initial fragment completes Toxino in an admonition not to rely on being young. The Portuguese confie- continues below, so the physical break is retained.
The warning against relying on youth ends here. A new example concerns one's own strength, with its final verb divided ta- / nomu.

runs.text: Confiar em minhas forças, ou poſſe.

lines.note: Nomu completes tanomu. The Portuguese explains relying on one's own strength or resources, and the double long s in poſſe is retained.
Tanomidocoro denotes support or refuge. Emparo is the historical source spelling and is not silently regularized to a modern Portuguese form.
Tanomigai is trust or hope grounded in something demonstrable. The final word leads into obras on the next line, specifying practical deeds.
The definition grounds trust in actions. The Japanese example describes a person lacking such reliability; its Portuguese translation appears on the following line.

runs.text: He homem em que ſe não pode confiar. ¶

lines.note: The example means a person who cannot be trusted. A contrasting positive example begins Ta- and continues below without changing entries.
The initial fragment completes Tanomigaino in the positive example. The Portuguese introduces someone in whom one can have confidence, with the explanation continuing below.

runs.text: ſe pode confiar; porque ordinariamente acode

lines.note: This person is trustworthy because he habitually comes to help. The grounds for reliability are practical assistance, whose circumstances are specified on the next line.
The person helps in times of need, completing the positive reliability example. The printed ß in neceßidades is retained as a source glyph.
This verbal entry means to trust someone completely. Its nasal abbreviations are preserved, and it remains separate from the following noun with the same stem.

runs.text: O confiar, ou eſtribar de todo em

lines.note: The noun Tanomiqiri names complete trust or reliance. The Portuguese complement continues below and introduces an example involving an only child.
The definition ends with reliance on someone. The Japanese example begins because this is my only child; it continues on the next physical line.
The Japanese example completes the statement of total reliance. Its Portuguese translation begins with this being the speaker's child and continues below.

runs.text: filho vnico, nelle tenho todo meu arrimo, &

lines.note: The only child is the speaker's entire support. The final conjunction requires the following body word encoſto, previously misclassified with the catchword.
Encoſto completes the Portuguese only-child example as another word for support. It is body text, not part of the adjacent Tanomi- catchword; the original stable ID is retained after relocation.
